It's a positive mood all around as European investors get to their desks this morning, with Spain's benchmark index leading gains in the early stages. The broader market mood is looking relatively upbeat, although I wouldn't read too much into the early advance just yet.

As a reminder, we are dealing with a partial market closure in the US to start the new week. Wall Street will remain open for business later but the bond market will be closed. That means traders and investors will be without one of the most important market signals to work with, especially as the surge higher in Treasury yields have been a key driver weighing on risk sentiment in recent weeks.

Besides that, thinner liquidity conditions could also exaggerate price movements across the board in the day ahead. So, the early gains may not necessarily signal much conviction among investors.

For now though, the overall risk mood is steadier and reflecting some mild optimism at the very least. US futures are also pointing up with both S&P 500 futures and Nasdaq futures higher by 0.2%.

But looking to the week ahead, there is reason for markets to adopt a more cautious mood in the days to come. The US CPI report on Wednesday is the key risk event to be mindful of, which could be pivotal in determining whether Treasury yields have another leg higher to go. A hotter-than-expected report would certainly make things dicey for stocks, especially if they reinforce expectations that the Fed may have to raise interest rates further.

As such, I would treat the positive open here as a welcome breather for markets. But whether or not this turns into something more concrete will depend on what happens when the bond market returns tomorrow and more importantly, how the US CPI report lands on Wednesday.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What is earnings season and why the first companies to report are important to watch
item.description:
Four times a year, publicly traded companies release their financial results, giving investors a picture of how businesses are performing, whether conditions are improving or deteriorating, and whether current stock prices are justified by future profit expectations.

For investors, earnings are about comparing actual results with expectations, assessing what management expects in the coming quarters, and determining whether the new information changes the outlook for future earnings.

What is earnings season?

Earnings season is a specific multi-week period each quarter when a vast majority of publicly traded companies cluster together to release their official financial earning (revenue, profits, and losses) and reports for the previous quarter. In the United States, it typically takes place four times a year, following the end of each fiscal quarter.

The main reporting periods generally fall in January and February, April and May, July and August, and October and November. The exact timing varies by company because businesses have different fiscal calendars and reporting deadlines.

During these periods, companies publish their quarterly earnings reports, which usually include an income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement, comparisons with previous periods, and management commentary. Many companies also hold earnings calls, where executives explain the results and answer questions from analysts and investors.

Earnings season attracts considerable attention because it provides a concentrated flow of new information about corporate profitability. Instead of receiving information about individual companies gradually throughout the quarter, investors receive results from hundreds of businesses over a relatively short period.

Image: Earnings Calendar for the current week on earningswhispers.com

In what order do companies report earnings?

There is no official order in which companies must report their results. Each company announces its own reporting date, subject to applicable disclosure rules and its fiscal calendar. Nevertheless, earnings season tends to follow a recognizable pattern.

Large US banks often report near the beginning of the season. JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup and Goldman Sachs are frequently among the early major reporters. Their results are followed by companies from other industries, including technology, industrials, consumer goods, healthcare and energy.

Large technology companies, such as Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, often report later in the season, although the exact order varies from quarter to quarter.

The first companies to report can also provide investors with an early indication of the economic conditions affecting their industries. Banks, for example, offer information about loan demand, credit quality, consumer finances, corporate borrowing and investment banking activity. Technology companies provide clues about business spending, cloud demand, advertising markets and investment in artificial intelligence. Retailers offer insight into consumer spending, pricing power and inventory conditions. 

Why can the first company to report move an entire sector?

The stock market is forward-looking. Investors do not value a company solely on its current profits. They estimate how much money it will generate in the future and discount those expected cash flows back to the present. This means that information about one company can influence the valuation of other companies exposed to similar economic conditions.

Imagine that a major US bank reports stronger than expected loan growth, resilient net interest income and lower than anticipated credit losses. Investors may conclude that the banking sector is benefiting from healthier borrowers and more favourable lending conditions. They could then raise their earnings expectations for other banks, even before those companies publish their own results, leading to a rise in stock prices.

The opposite can happen if a company reports deteriorating demand, rising costs or weaker guidance. Investors may assume that other businesses facing similar conditions could experience the same problems. 

Companies in the same sector share common economic drivers. Banks are sensitive to interest rates, credit conditions and loan demand. Semiconductor companies are exposed to chip demand, capital expenditure and inventory cycles. Retailers depend on consumer spending, wages and pricing power. Information from one company can therefore reveal something about the environment facing its competitors.

Moreover, many investment funds trade entire sectors through exchange-traded funds, baskets of stocks and sector-specific strategies. A change in the perceived outlook for an industry can therefore generate buying or selling across several companies at once.

Keep in mind, though, that the reaction is not always uniform. A company may benefit from market-share gains at the expense of competitors, or it may have company-specific problems that do not affect the rest of the sector. Investors need to distinguish between information that reflects a broad industry trend from information unique to the reporting company.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Market playbook: What if US CPI comes in hot but stocks refuse to fall?
item.description:
The main focus in markets this week will be on the US CPI report due Wednesday, 14 October. The inflation numbers for September will be heavily scrutinised as traders and investors are very much still caught in trying to weigh the inflation outlook as well as risks of the Fed raising interest rates further. And all of that is made even more crucial as Treasury yields are threatening multi-decade highs in the past week or so.

The usual expectation is that a hotter-than-expected inflation report will be bad news for stocks. But what if we actually get that but Wall Street refuses to play ball and stocks do not happen to fall? That is a rather interesting scenario, no?

To start, let's just consider what the typical market reaction should be. Higher inflation would mean that the Fed might have to keep interest rates "higher for longer" or even raise them further to deal with stronger price pressures in general.

As things stand, Fed funds futures are currently pricing in roughly an 81% probability that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged later this month. As such, a hotter-than-expected inflation report could challenge that pricing expectations and see traders push for bets on another rate hike. If not, it could at least reinforce expectations of another move in December.

In turn, that rightfully should translate to higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. And for stocks, that's usually not a good combination to deal with. Higher yields make borrowing more expensive for companies while also making bonds more attractive relative to equities. In turn, that could put downward pressure on stock valuations, particularly among big tech.

However, what happens if the market reaction isn't what we expect it to be and stocks don't move according to how they should? How should we approach that as a trader?

Well, the first is to understand what might be causing such a market reaction. Perhaps it is a case that traders had already positioned themselves for a hot inflation reading, meaning much of the bad news was priced in beforehand. Or it could be a case of the devil being in the details, with the headline number looking ugly but the underlying inflation details aren't quite as worrying.

Having said that, I'd still be wary of immediately treating that resilience as a bullish signal. The thing I want to see is whether stocks can build on the initial reaction, especially if Treasury yields continue climbing. Sure, stocks might hold firmer in the first 15 to 30 minutes after the data. But if yields keep pushing higher and equities start losing ground a couple of hours later, then perhaps that initial resilience wasn't quite as convincing as it first appeared.

Besides that, it will also be worth watching whether the buying in the stock market is more broad-based or merely supported by a handful of big tech names. That will provide some idea of what is actually carrying the market mood in equities should there be contradicting signals from the likes of bonds and the dollar.

So, don't just focus and trade on the headline numbers from the US CPI report. It would be wise to also pay attention to how markets react in the hours that follow as the absence of a selloff can arguably tell us more than the inflation numbers themselves.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold futures swing trade idea: Four buy entries and four upside targets
item.description:
Gold futures swing trade idea: A patient buy ladder with four upside targets

Gold futures (GC/MGC) | October 12, 2026 | Multi-week swing trade

Gold futures are trading near $4,215 in the supplied October 12 snapshot, following a substantial correction from the late-August highs near $4,755. Although a bullish reversal is not yet confirmed, buyers appear to be defending the broader $4,100 to $4,160 region. My preferred approach is to wait for lower prices and build a position gradually, rather than chase the recovery.

The strategy involves four potential buy entries, a defined protective stop and four profit targets. Larger allocations are reserved for deeper pullbacks, but some orders may never execute.

Swing trade at a glance

Weighted-average entry: $4,172.98Assumes all four orders fill.Protective stop: $4,126.60Trade exit level, not proof that the wider support region has failed.Blended reward-to-risk: 4.27:13 / 3 / 3 / 1 target allocation.Planned gross risk: $4,638Ten Micro Gold contracts; excludes commissions, slippage and gaps.

Building the position: Four buy orders

Rather than entering the full position near $4,215, the proposed strategy distributes 10 Micro Gold futures contracts (MGC) across four lower prices. Together, they equal the exposure of one standard GC contract. The bars show each order’s share of the full position, not a forecast for gold prices.

Buy 1 | $4,198.60   1 micro contract (10%)Buy 2 | $4,194.50   2 micro contracts (20%)Buy 3 | $4,169.80   3 micro contracts (30%)Buy 4 | $4,158.20   4 micro contracts (40%)Full-position weighted-average entry: $4,172.98

A shallow correction creates only limited exposure, while a deeper pullback allows a larger position at more favorable prices. But a lower average does not automatically make a trade safer. Falling prices can also indicate that sellers are getting stronger. Gold could instead rebound without reaching the lower orders, leaving a smaller position with a different average entry and risk profile.

Four upside targets for a possible gold recovery

Profit targets and reward-to-risk

TP1: $4,257 | 1.81:1An initial recovery objective and opportunity to consider partial profits.TP2: $4,338 | 3.56:1A more meaningful repair of the bearish structure.TP3: $4,425 | 5.43:1A stronger recovery supporting improving bullish momentum.TP4, runner: $4,648 | 10.24:1An ambitious move toward the region of the preceding highs.

These reward-to-risk ratios assume all ten entries are filled and use the resulting weighted-average entry. An equal 25% allocation to the four targets would produce approximately 5.26:1. But ten contracts cannot be split evenly across four targets in whole contracts. A practical alternative is to exit three at TP1, three at TP2, three at TP3 and one at TP4. That yields a blended 4.27:1.

Potential gross profit by target

The following bar comparison illustrates profit contributions for the 3 / 3 / 3 / 1 exits if all entry orders fill and every exit order executes as planned. Amounts are in U.S. dollars and exclude transaction costs.

TP1 (3 contracts): $2,520.60TP2 (3 contracts): $4,950.60TP3 (3 contracts): $7,560.60TP4 (1 contract): $4,750.20

Illustrative financial outcomes

Potential total gross profit: $19,782Only if all four targets are realized at their planned prices.Planned total gross loss: -$4,638If all ten contracts fill and the stop executes at its stated price.Blended reward-to-risk: 4.27:1A payoff ratio, not a success probability or expected return.

Trade management after the first profit target

The initial stop at $4,126.60 is $46.38 below the full-position average entry. If gold reaches TP1 at $4,257, I would consider reducing exposure and moving the remaining stop toward the actual weighted-average entry, subject to the filled orders and prevailing price structure. At TP2, protecting accumulated gains becomes increasingly important if a smaller runner remains.

Moving a stop toward entry does not guarantee a breakeven result. Gold futures can move rapidly, and execution prices, fees and gaps all affect outcomes.

What would strengthen or weaken this gold recovery?

Scenarios to watch

Recovery gaining credibility: Buyers defend the intended entriesHigher lows and a sustained move toward $4,257 and $4,338 would support an improving recovery, although the four-hour trend still needs confirmation.The trade thesis deteriorates: Selling continues through the buy areaFilling more lower entries could reflect weakening support. $4,126.60 is the planned trade stop even though it sits within the wider $4,100 to $4,160 region.The market rallies without us: Some buy orders never fillA missed entry is not a reason to chase price or assume that the original full-position calculations still apply.

Why patience matters for this multi-week gold trade

The targets require progressively greater improvement in the price structure, particularly the ambitious final runner at $4,648. Meanwhile, upcoming U.S. inflation figures could influence Treasury yields, the dollar and gold futures, producing further volatility before a sustainable recovery develops.

There are two distinct questions: Can gold stabilize sufficiently for a patient entry? And can it then recover far enough to reach the distant targets? The first does not establish the second.

For me, the attraction is the combination of selective entries, measured exposure and several opportunities to take profits, not a certainty that gold will revisit $4,648. I would rather miss the first leg of a rally than abandon the entry plan because price moves higher without me.

What I'm also watching:

while bullion is attempting to gain traction, Eamonn at investingLive.com highlighted that gold's move higher in Asia on the Russia-Ukraine energy truce narrative rests on very shaky support, especially with Kyiv reporting fresh infrastructure strikes within hours and the core macro focus remaining tied to crude prices ahead of Wednesday's US CPI.

From a technical standpoint, as Justin from investingLive.com noted, gold buyers eyeing a decisive $4,200 breakout still face major hurdles around $4,220 and $4,256, meaning upside momentum will need sustained order flow and a clear reclaim of overhead resistance to confirm a lasting recovery.

item.title: Macro pulse: US bank earnings could reveal the hidden cost of surging Treasury yields
item.description:
It's earnings season again and as is always the case, the big banks on Wall Street will be the ones to kick start proceedings starting tomorrow.

While much of the usual focus will be on whether the banks manage to beat earnings expectations, there is perhaps a more important story running in the background this time around. That being how the recent surge in Treasury yields is impacting the banking sector and, by extension, the broader US economy.

Now, higher interest rates and yields aren't necessarily a bad thing for banks to begin with. They can charge more interest on loans and that potentially means fatter margins to work with in trying to earn more money. However, there's also the other side of the equation to be mindful about.

Higher borrowing costs are also likely to weigh more on demand conditions, in particular demand for loans. Just think about businesses deciding to hold back on expansion plans or households putting off from taking up a new mortgage because financing has become too expensive.

As such, that will be one of the key things to watch in the earnings reports this week.

Besides that, banks will also have to face higher funding costs as they may need to offer better deposit rates to keep customers from moving their money elsewhere. So even if lending income improves, that doesn't automatically translate to better profit margins.

And then there's also the question of credit quality. If borrowers struggle to keep up with repayments, banks could start seeing more missed payments and potentially higher loan losses. Any clues pointing in this direction would offer another indication to markets that tighter financial conditions are starting to take a toll on businesses and/or households.

Now of course, none of this means that we're starting to see major problems emerge in the banking sector. However, they do offer markets a useful gauge on whether the impact of higher yields is starting to filter through to the real economy.

So, don't just pay attention to how much money the banks are making this week. It'll be worth paying just as much attention to signs on whether their customers are starting to feel the pinch.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price eyes $4,200 breakout, but buyers still face two major hurdles
item.description:
Gold buyers are making another attempt to decisively get above the $4,200 level to start the new week. The precious metal touched a high of $4,217 earlier in Asia trading but is now trickling back lower to the figure level again, which has been a key point of contention since last week already.

The region around $4,200-20 has been causing quite a bit of frustration for buyers, so I wouldn't say that gold has convinced of any break to the upside just yet. Having said that, there are at least some encouraging signs for buyers since the end of last week.

Looking at the hourly chart, gold had managed to climb above both its 100-hour (red line) and 200-hour (blue line) moving averages on Friday and is sticking with that for now. That is a welcome development for buyers, especially after having struggled to build any real momentum in recent weeks. So, the price move here suggests that the near-term technical picture is at least looking more constructive. However, there is still some work to be done.

Despite the near-term bias siding with buyers now, they are still unable to really shake off the $4,200 level. Besides that, they have to also contend with swing region resistance closer to $4,220. That has been a stumbling block for any upside pushes so far this month, so getting past that would offer a stronger signal that buyers are attempting a stronger recovery.

But even then, the daily chart presents another challenge not too far away.

The 100-day moving average (red line) around $4,256 remains a key technical hurdle to any upside momentum. Unless buyers can also firmly break above that, I will be hesitant to suggest that the rebound in gold since the end of last week has much legs to run.

On the flip side though, another rejection around $4,200-20 could see sellers step back into the picture with more confidence. That will turn back the focus on the key hourly moving averages around $4,148-56 next before potentially eyeing the supportive region around $4,100-17 from the end September and early October lows.

For now, getting above $4,200 is the first step that buyers need to take to establish some footing. However, getting past $4,220 and $4,256 is where the real test begins.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Can TSMC keep the AI boom running as US CPI looms?
item.description:
Q3 earnings season in Wall Street will kick off in earnest this week, as the big banks will begin reporting their quarterly results starting tomorrow. While that will hog some of the spotlight in the stock market, the AI boom continues to be one of the more closely watched themes. As such, I would pick TSMC as the stock to pay attention to in terms of earnings releases in the days ahead.

The big question now among investors with regards to the AI boom is whether all the spending on chips and data centers can keep going.

So, TSMC might offer a better idea of that when they report their earnings on Thursday, 15 October. As a reminder, TSMC is one of the biggest chip manufacturers in the world and plays a crucial role in the AI supply chain. Nvidia might be the more familiar household name as they design powerful chips needed to run AI applications, but someone still has to manufacture them. And that is where TSMC comes in.

Analysts are expecting EPS of around $4.42 for its US-listed shares, with net profit projected to surge roughly 65% to NT$746.3 billion.

Now, TSMC has already enjoyed a rather impressive quarter. The firm reported record revenue of NT$1.49 trillion ($46.7 billion), which is up 50% from a year ago and beating market expectations of NT$1.46 trillion. But with expectations already running so high, I would argue that it is definitely a very tall order to impress investors further from this point. In other words, investors might be looking for more than just another record-breaking quarter to be satisfied.

As such, there will be watchful eyes on whether TSMC can keep this momentum up heading into 2027. What the firm says about AI chip demand and whether customers are still looking to ramp up orders might be more important than the headline numbers themselves.

But before we even get to TSMC's earnings this week, there is also the broader market picture to consider.

The US CPI report on Wednesday will arguably be the bigger key risk event for markets this week. And with Treasury yields staying elevated, another hot inflation reading could put further pressure on tech stocks - regardless of how well TSMC performs.

Taking that into account, I reckon an upbeat outlook from TSMC could still offer some reassurance that the AI boom has room to run. However, whether that will be enough to keep AI stocks rallying is another question altogether.

I mean, investors are already paying a hefty premium for AI-related stocks. So, they might not have that much appetite to keep paying such high prices if inflation worries and rising bond yields continue to weigh on broader market sentiment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • The earnings call, with fourth-quarter and full-year guidance, is on Thursday at 06:00 GMT (2:00 am ET)
  • Third-quarter revenue rose 50% year on year to a record, beating forecasts
  • Morgan Stanley expects TSMC to lift its full-year revenue growth forecast to the low-to-mid 40% range
  • Analysts expect questions on a possible Texas expansion, after Elon Musk said TSMC could sublease part of his Terafab complex

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co is expected to report a sixth consecutive quarter of record profit on Thursday, driven by surging technology-sector spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure, Reuters reported.

The world’s largest maker of advanced AI chips is forecast to post a 65% rise in third-quarter net profit to around T$746 billion ($23 billion), according to an LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 16 analysts, which gives more weight to historically accurate forecasters. Any result above about T$707 billion would be the company’s highest-ever quarterly profit and its 11th straight quarter of growth. TSMC already reported last week that third-quarter revenue rose 50% year on year to a record, beating expectations.

Analysts say demand remains strong for both TSMC’s AI chipmaking capacity and CoWoS, its advanced packaging technology that combines processors and memory into a single high-performance unit, a critical step in building AI accelerators. That demand has made TSMC, a key supplier to Nvidia and Apple, Asia’s most valuable company, with a market value of around $2.1 trillion, almost double that of South Korean rival Samsung Electronics.

Guidance will be the main focus. The company will give fourth-quarter and updated full-year forecasts on its earnings call at 06:00 GMT (2:00 am ET). Morgan Stanley analyst Charlie Chan expects TSMC to raise its full-year revenue growth forecast to the low-to-mid 40% range, from more than 40% currently, on strong demand for its 3-nanometre chips. In July, TSMC lifted its capital spending forecast for this year to between $60 billion and $64 billion.

Analysts also expect questions about expansion in Texas. TSMC is investing $265 billion in chip plants in Arizona, and Reuters reported in September that it was evaluating a Texas investment. Elon Musk said last week that his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing part of it. Chan said Texas could become necessary given demand and limited space in Arizona within five years, while another equity analyst saw little urgency because some planned Arizona fabs have yet to be built, describing Texas as a longer-term option.

TSMC’s Taipei-listed shares have risen 63% this year, broadly in line with the 69% gain in Taiwan’s broader market, leaving guidance as the likely driver of the stock’s reaction.

item.title: Early Ethereum Foundation ETH recipients move $11M to Kraken: what the data shows
item.description:
Early Ethereum Foundation ETH recipients move $11M to Kraken: what the data shows

Two wallets that received Ether (ETH) from an early Ethereum Foundation distribution sent 4,393 ETH, worth about $11.1 million, to the Kraken exchange on Monday, according to on-chain tracker Lookonchain. The transfers prompted questions on social media about whether the Foundation is selling again. The wallet history on Arkham Intelligence supports a more cautious reading: the coins are two steps removed from the Foundation, and an exchange deposit is not the same as a sale.

What the wallet trail shows

Arkham data shows the Ethereum Foundation sent 59,751 ETH to an intermediary address about a decade ago, when ETH traded near $0.90. That address later split the coins into three parcels of roughly 18,000 ETH each and sent them to separate wallets, at a time when ETH was worth about $2.13.

One of those three wallets made the largest of Monday’s deposits, about 2,998 ETH, or around $7.6 million. Based on Lookonchain’s total, the second wallet accounts for roughly 1,395 ETH.

None of the downstream addresses is labelled as a Foundation wallet on Arkham. Equal parcels fit a pattern of ETH being distributed to separate recipients, but the data does not show who controls the wallets.

This is also not the first time the main wallet has used Kraken. Roughly five years ago it sent about 4,000 ETH to Kraken deposit addresses, in batches of 1,000 and 2,000 ETH.

Why the distinction matters

The Ethereum Foundation has sold ETH from its own treasury in the past, so trackers watch any address connected to it closely. A wallet that received Foundation ETH years ago is not necessarily controlled by the Foundation today, in the same way that a former employee selling shares is not the company selling.

An exchange deposit makes a sale possible and often comes before one. The blockchain, however, only records that the coins reached a Kraken deposit address. What happens to them inside the exchange is not publicly visible.

Scale matters too. About $11 million is small against ETH’s typical daily trading volume, so this flow is unlikely to drive the price on its own. The more relevant question is what happens to the coins still held. Based on the transfers visible on Arkham, the main wallet may still hold around 11,000 ETH from its original allocation, and the other two parcels from the same split could hold more.

What to watch next

  • Wallet labels: if Arkham or the Foundation ties these addresses to the Foundation itself, the story changes materially.
  • Remaining balances: further deposits from these wallets or their sister addresses would make a potential supply overhang a fairer question.
  • Official disclosure: a Foundation statement on treasury sales would be the clearest confirmation either way.
This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Indian Rupee set for 1% rally as RBI curbs hedging rush that hit a record $77 billion
item.description:
The rupee’s weakness is largely an energy story: high crude prices have swollen India’s import bill and dollar demand, and the RBI’s special window for oil marketing companies is an admission that fuel purchases are a core source of pressure. That makes the rally vulnerable to any renewed rise in crude, including from weekend attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Higher hedging costs should ease near-term dollar buying and pull forward premiums lower, offering some support to Asian currencies more broadly. Sustained gains likely depend on foreign equity outflows slowing, since administrative curbs have historically offered only temporary relief.

---

The RBI has made it more expensive to bet against the rupee, but it can’t make oil any cheaper.

Summary:

  • The rupee surged in the offshore non-deliverable forward market, signalling a rally of about 1% from Friday’s close near 96.7 per dollar when onshore trading opens Monday
  • The RBI is asking banks to hold reserves against large hedges and limiting the rebooking of cancelled rupee derivative contracts
  • Bankers say the measures could raise hedging costs by 80 to 150 basis points
  • Corporate forward-dollar purchases hit a record $77 billion in September, up 80% from a year earlier
  • The RBI is also letting oil marketing companies buy dollars directly from the central bank through a special window
  • The rupee, down nearly 7% this year, came close to its record low of just under 97 last week

The Indian rupee is set for a sharp rebound on Monday after the Reserve Bank of India stepped up efforts to curb dollar demand, with offshore trading pointing to a gain of about 1% from Friday’s close near 96.7 per dollar.

The one-month dollar/rupee non-deliverable forward contract signalled the rupee could rally past 96 when onshore markets open at 9 am in Mumbai (03:30 GMT, 11:30 pm ET Sunday). Non-deliverable forwards are offshore contracts settled in dollars, allowing investors to trade the rupee outside India and often giving an early read on where the currency will open.

The rally follows new RBI measures aimed at slowing a surge in corporate hedging against further rupee weakness. Banks will be asked to hold reserves against large hedges, and the common practice of cancelling and rebooking rupee-linked derivative contracts will be restricted. Six bankers said the measures could raise hedging costs by 80 to 150 basis points, depending on how much banks pass on to clients, and are designed to make speculative positioning harder.

The scale of hedging shows why the RBI acted. Corporate purchases of forward dollars rose to a record $77 billion in September, up 80% from a year earlier, while sales were far smaller at $41 billion, adding to pressure on the currency. The curbs caught markets off guard, with bankers working through the weekend to put systems in place for Monday’s open.

The central bank has also opened a special window allowing oil marketing companies to buy dollars directly from it, targeting one of the largest sources of daily dollar demand. India imports most of its crude, so the surge in oil prices tied to the Middle East conflict has fed directly into its import bill.

The rupee has been Asia’s worst-performing currency this year, down nearly 7%, under pressure from high oil prices and heavy foreign outflows from Indian equities. It came close to its record low of just under 97 last week, despite about $140 billion raised through special dollar deposit schemes and higher interest rates.

A currency adviser cautioned that such measures have historically had limited staying power unless the underlying pressures ease. Whether the rally holds is likely to depend on the path of oil prices and foreign investment flows rather than on the RBI’s latest curbs.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold edges up in Asia on the energy truce narrative, that looks like a VERY shaky support
item.description:
For gold, the key channel in this conflict has been oil rather than safe-haven demand: escalation has lifted energy prices and Fed hike expectations, pushing up yields and the dollar and weighing on bullion. On that logic, a credible energy truce would be supportive, but this one was disputed within hours and has not been confirmed by Moscow, so a rally built on it rests on weak foundations. A breakdown would likely put Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries back in play, tightening diesel supply and reinforcing the inflation pressure that has hurt gold. Wednesday’s US CPI and Gulf attacks, which move oil far more, are the stronger drivers.

---

Gold’s logic in this war is simple: lower oil helps it, so a truce should too, but not one that was disputed before the day was out.

Summary:

  • Gold edged higher in Asian trade on Monday, with some market chatter attributing the move to Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire
  • Zelenskyy said Russia struck the CHP-5 power plant in Kharkiv and a plant in Kyiv hours after the truce was announced on Sunday
  • The Kremlin has not commented, and neither side appears to have publicly confirmed the terms before Trump’s announcement
  • Ukraine says it will stop striking Russian energy facilities if Russia does the same
  • Previous Trump-brokered energy pauses, in spring 2025 and earlier this year, failed to last
  • US CPI on Wednesday and Fed Chair Warsh’s remarks on Friday are likely to matter more for gold

Gold edged higher in Asian trade on Monday, trading above $4,200 an ounce, with some market chatter crediting the move to Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. The narrative looks fragile: within hours of the announcement, Kyiv said Russia had struck Ukrainian power plants, and Moscow has yet to say whether it agreed to the truce at all.

Trump announced on Sunday that both sides had agreed to an immediate halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. That evening, Russia struck the CHP-5 thermal power plant in Kharkiv, according to Ukrainian officials, with a local official telling ABC News it was hit at least twice and caught fire. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a plant in Kyiv was also targeted, and that Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission over the past week. The Kremlin had not commented at the time of writing, and Ukrainian officials said they learned of the deal from Trump’s social media post.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine supports the truce and would stop striking Russian energy facilities if Russia did the same. Similar arrangements have broken down before: a 30-day moratorium brokered by Trump in spring 2025 did not last, and a week-long pause on strikes against Kyiv’s energy system ended on February 1 this year with renewed attacks.

The link between the truce and gold runs through energy prices rather than safe-haven demand. Throughout the Iran war, escalation has tended to hurt bullion by lifting oil, raising inflation expectations and strengthening the case for further Federal Reserve hikes, which pushes up yields and the dollar. On that logic, a lasting energy truce would be positive for gold by easing fuel prices. The problem is that this truce was disputed within hours, and a Russia-Ukraine energy pause is a much smaller factor for oil than supply from the Gulf.

The pattern was visible last week. Gold rose more than 1% on Thursday as oil fell and the dollar softened after Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. By the same token, weekend attacks on Saudi Arabia, including Houthi claims of strikes on Aramco facilities, are a risk for gold if they push crude higher. Bullion is still around 25% below its January record near $5,600 and has slipped about 2% over the past month.

The bigger tests come later in the week. US consumer price data on Wednesday (preview one, preview two) will shape expectations for an October Fed hike, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks early on Friday. A firm inflation reading would likely matter far more for gold than a ceasefire that appears to have been disputed within hours of being announced.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s growth stocks lose their shine as CICC tilts towards dividend payers
item.description:
For China’s equity markets, CICC’s call points to continued rotation from high-flying growth names on the ChiNext and STAR boards towards dividend-paying stocks, a group typically dominated by banks, utilities, energy and telecom companies. That could support relative strength in dividend indexes even if the broader market stays volatile. The trigger points are largely external: US inflation data and Fed signals this week bear on the overseas liquidity concerns CICC cites, while Middle East escalation and doubts over AI spending would weigh most on the technology half of the trade. A strong run of global chip earnings could revive appetite for growth names and narrow the case for defensive positioning.

---

Earlier:

  • PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
  • Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal

---

After a tech-led first half, CICC wants investors in China to hold their growth stocks in one hand and something steadier in the other.

Summary:

  • CICC says A-share technology growth stocks rallied in the first half of 2026, driven by the AI supply chain and high-end manufacturing
  • Since July, negative narratives around the global AI chain, expectations of tighter overseas liquidity and Middle East risk have triggered a notable correction in previously strong growth sectors
  • With growth-stock volatility higher and risk appetite weaker, the firm says the case for dividend-paying assets deserves re-evaluation
  • It expects a “technology plus dividends” dumbbell allocation to gain emphasis as a way to balance earnings growth, shareholder cash returns and stability
  • CICC favours tech companies with clear industry trends, durable advantages and proven earnings, and dividend stocks with stable cash flow, sustainable payouts and reasonable valuations

China International Capital Corp expects investors in China’s mainland stock market to place greater emphasis on a “technology plus dividends” dumbbell strategy, after a sharp pullback in growth stocks since July exposed the risks of a portfolio tilted heavily towards tech.

A dumbbell, or barbell, strategy concentrates holdings at two ends of the risk spectrum rather than in the middle: in this case, higher-growth technology stocks on one side and stable, dividend-paying companies on the other. The aim is to capture upside from structural growth themes while relying on dividend payers to cushion portfolios when markets turn volatile. 

In a research note, CICC said A-share technology growth stocks benefited in the first half of 2026 from strong conditions across the AI supply chain and high-end manufacturing, sustaining a structural rally. Since July, however, three pressures have combined to drive a notable correction in those previously strong sectors: rising negative narratives around the global AI industry chain, expectations of tighter overseas liquidity and increased geopolitical risk in the Middle East.

The liquidity concern reflects the global rate backdrop. The US Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September and markets are still weighing whether further increases will follow, making this week’s US inflation data and remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh relevant to Chinese equities as well.

With growth-stock volatility higher and risk appetite weaker, CICC said the relative appeal of dividend assets deserves a fresh look. It argued that in an environment where overall growth is limited but pockets of strong structural growth remain, and where risk sentiment swings sharply, combining technology with dividends offers a way to balance earnings growth potential, shareholder cash returns and portfolio stability.

On implementation, the firm recommends focusing on technology companies with clear industry trends, durable competitive advantages and a demonstrated ability to deliver profits. For the dividend side, it favours high-quality companies with stable earnings and cash flow, sustainable payout policies and reasonable valuations.

Whether the rotation deepens is likely to depend on the external triggers CICC identified, particularly the direction of US monetary policy and how the global AI earnings season unfolds over the coming weeks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Deutsche Bank’s CEO warns wins for AfD and Left in 3 state votes risk deterring investors
item.description:
For the DAX, Sewing’s remarks are unlikely to move the index on their own, since state governments do not set federal economic policy and the index is dominated by global exporters whose earnings depend more on world demand than on domestic politics. The more direct exposure is in German residential property stocks, where the Left Party’s expropriation pledge in Berlin adds headline risk to listed landlords with large holdings in the capital. Over time, a perception of rising political risk could add to the discount investors already apply to German assets, making the pace of Merz’s reforms a more important driver for domestically focused DAX and MDAX names.

---

Germany’s top banker is warning that investors don’t read the fine print of federalism: a shock in one state looks like a shock to the whole country.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank Chief Executive Christian Sewing said the rise of parties on the political extremes poses a significant risk to Germany and should not be played down
  • The AfD came close to an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt and took first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania last month
  • The Left Party scored its biggest win in Berlin’s city election, pledging to expropriate the holdings of residential property companies
  • Sewing said foreign investors are unlikely to distinguish between a state government and Germany as a whole
  • He urged Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to continue reforms to revive the economy, calling it the only answer to extremes on both sides

The head of Germany’s largest bank has warned that recent state election victories for parties on the political extremes could drive away foreign investors, urging the federal government to keep pressing ahead with economic reforms.

Deutsche Bank Chief Executive Christian Sewing told the Bild daily (info via Reuters) that the rise of the far right and far left poses a significant risk to Germany that should not be downplayed. He argued that foreign investors cannot be expected to draw a clear line between a single state government and the country as a whole, and said that perception was understandable from an investor’s point of view.

The comments follow a series of state elections last month. The AfD, which wants to restrict immigration and return asylum seekers, and which security services classify as extremist in some regions, narrowly missed an absolute majority in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt. Two weeks later, it took first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In Berlin, the Left Party won its biggest victory in the city government election on a pledge to tackle soaring housing costs by expropriating the holdings of residential property companies.

Sewing said developments in both Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin were neither conducive to economic growth nor investment-friendly. Economists have also accused the AfD of fostering a climate that could deter the skilled workers and foreign capital the German economy needs.

The Berlin pledge revives a long-running debate in the capital. Berlin voters backed a non-binding 2021 referendum calling for large landlords’ flats to be taken into public ownership, though it was never implemented. The Left Party’s win puts the issue back on the agenda with a party in a stronger position to pursue it.

Sewing called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to continue its reform programme, describing it as the only response to extremists on both the right and left. The warning lands as Germany’s economy struggles to regain momentum, with investors watching whether Berlin can deliver reforms quickly enough to offset concerns about the political climate.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

The core reading is the trigger for rates markets: an in-line 0.2% would likely keep October hike pricing subdued and leave the dollar and Treasury yields range-bound, while a repeat of August’s 0.3% would revive bets on a back-to-back move and lift the front end. Warsh’s comments early Friday could then reset expectations either way ahead of the October 27-28 meeting.

---

Energy is doing the damage to the headline; the Fed’s real question this week is whether anything else is starting to burn.

Summary:

  • MUFG expects US headline inflation to rise to 3.6% in September, driven almost entirely by higher energy prices since the US-Iran conflict began
  • Core inflation is forecast to ease to 0.2% month on month after August’s services-driven 0.3% rise
  • MUFG says another upside surprise in core would likely be needed to revive expectations of a back-to-back Fed hike this month
  • Retail sales on Thursday are expected to confirm that consumer spending grew strongly in the third quarter
  • Fed Chair Warsh speaks at the IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok early Friday, his first public remarks since the September FOMC meeting

Wednesday’s US inflation report is the main economic release of the week, and MUFG says the key question is not how high headline inflation climbs but whether price pressures are beginning to spread beyond energy.

The bank expects the September consumer price index to show headline inflation rising to 3.6%. It notes that the increase since the start of the US-Iran conflict has been driven almost entirely by higher energy prices, so the Federal Reserve and markets will focus on core inflation for any tentative signs of broadening. The report is due at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET).

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, picked up to 0.3% month on month in August, led by services. MUFG expects it to ease back to 0.2% in September. The bank says another upside surprise would likely be needed to revive market expectations of a back-to-back rate hike as soon as this month, following the Fed’s increase to a 3.75% to 4.00% target range in September.

Those expectations have already faded. Bets on an October move fell sharply after September payrolls showed only 29,000 jobs added, leaving a December hike as the market’s main scenario. A firm core reading would challenge that view; an in-line one would likely reinforce it.

Retail sales for September, due on Thursday at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET), are expected to confirm that consumer spending continued to grow strongly in the third quarter, a sign the economy has so far absorbed higher energy costs and tighter policy.

The week ends with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is scheduled to take part in a fireside chat at the IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok at around 04:30 GMT on Friday (00:30 ET). He has not spoken publicly since the September meeting, so his remarks will be scrutinised for guidance ahead of the October 27-28 decision. Warsh has moved the Fed away from explicit forward guidance, so markets are likely to focus on his tone on inflation rather than any signal on timing.
