item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China publishes its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time the previous evening), and the number has become one of the most closely followed signals in Asian currency markets. Its importance has grown over the past month as Beijing has moved from holding back the yuan’s rise to steering it gradually higher.

---

Earlier:

  • Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal

---

Under China’s managed float, the onshore yuan may trade up to 2% either side of the midpoint set each morning. The central bank arrives at that midpoint by weighing the previous session’s close, moves in the US dollar and other major currencies, wider global FX conditions, and domestic priorities including capital flows, growth and financial stability. Because the calculation leaves room for judgement, the fixing doubles as a tool for shaping expectations.

Once the rate is published, onshore trading proceeds within the band. If pressure drives the yuan toward either limit, the PBOC can respond by buying or selling the currency directly, adjusting liquidity, or acting through state-owned banks. That is why markets treat the fixing as a statement of intent. A midpoint stronger than forecast usually signals resistance to depreciation, while a weaker one can point to acceptance of a softer yuan, or discomfort with how quickly it is gaining.

For close to a year, the second message prevailed. The PBOC consistently set the midpoint weaker than market forecasts, which traders took as an effort to slow appreciation. That gap was at its widest since February in late August, soon after the yuan hit a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.

September marked a turning point. The central bank lifted the fixing for eight sessions in a row, its longest run since 2023, taking the midpoint to its strongest since February 2023. The onshore yuan climbed to levels last seen in January 2023 and the offshore rate to its firmest since July 2022. Yet the fixing is still being set well below estimates, at one point by more than 500 pips against a Reuters survey, suggesting Beijing is easing the brakes rather than releasing them.

Goldman Sachs analysts tied the firmer fixings to the run-up to the recent Trump-Xi summit, a pattern they said matches past diplomacy, and expect policymakers to remain comfortable with steady, gradual gains.

The trade-off has not changed. A stronger yuan supports capital stability and lowers import costs, but rapid gains could hurt exporters while the domestic economy remains soft. The daily gap between the fixing and consensus forecasts remains the clearest guide to how far Beijing will let the yuan run, and whether that tolerance outlasts the summit

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS: AI demand holds firm, with hyperscaler cloud growth tipped to hit 58%
item.description:
For equities, UBS’s view supports semiconductor and hardware names into an earnings season where results, rather than narrative, are expected to drive the AI trade. The near-term test arrives quickly, with ASML reporting on Wednesday and the major cloud providers later in the month, and any shortfall against the accelerating cloud growth UBS expects would likely hit richly valued megacaps hardest. Rates add a second risk: a hot US inflation print on Wednesday that lifts Treasury yields would weigh on long-duration tech valuations regardless of fundamentals. UBS’s preference for quality and defensive tech reflects that risk of sharp swings even within a supportive backdrop.

- UBS still sees the AI boom running on real demand, but after nearly five years it wants investors to be pickier about where they ride it.

Summary:

  • UBS says recent industry data continue to point to robust demand for AI compute and infrastructure
  • Meta’s Muse AI assistant has recorded more than 6.6 million downloads and 1.8 million daily active users in its first month, according to Sensor Tower data
  • TSMC reported a 51% rise in quarterly revenue, Samsung flagged an almost ninefold jump in operating profit, Hon Hai beat sales estimates and Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast
  • UBS expects average hyperscaler cloud revenue growth of 58% in the September quarter, up from 48% in the June quarter
  • The bank warns concerns over growth, financing and safety could cause bouts of volatility
  • It recommends a diversified approach favouring quality chip and hardware names, megacap platforms and defensive tech

Demand for artificial intelligence remains robust and fundamentals are likely to drive the AI trade through the coming earnings season, according to UBS, which pointed to strong chipmaker results and early signs of consumer appetite for AI agents.

The bank highlighted Meta’s Muse AI assistant, which has recorded more than 6.6 million downloads and 1.8 million daily active users since its launch a month ago, according to data from Sensor Tower. AI agents are tools that can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf rather than simply answering questions. UBS said it was too early to judge uptake of other recently launched agents, but described the early numbers as an encouraging sign that wider adoption could add further to AI demand.

Semiconductor results point the same way. TSMC reported a 51% rise in quarterly revenue, while Samsung flagged an almost ninefold jump in quarterly operating profit ahead of its full results. AI server assembler Hon Hai Precision Industry beat sales estimates, and chip designer Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast. UBS expects third-quarter earnings to provide further evidence of strong demand for AI compute and infrastructure.

Monetisation by the hyperscalers, the largest cloud computing providers, will be a key focus. UBS expects their average cloud revenue growth to accelerate to 58% year on year in the September quarter from 48% in the June quarter. It sees consumer AI agents as a potential next growth driver, opening revenue streams from subscriptions, advertising and transactions, and argues broader adoption would lift cloud utilisation, creating a clearer link between heavy infrastructure spending and revenue.

UBS acknowledged the risks. As the AI trade approaches its fifth year, it said concerns over growth, financing and safety could continue to trigger periods of volatility. It advised investors to stay engaged with what it sees as a structural opportunity while becoming more selective, favouring a diversified approach built around high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries of AI spending, megacap platforms and defensive technology companies.

The view will be tested quickly, with ASML reporting on Wednesday and the major cloud providers due later in the month.

---

Key terms explained

AI agents: Software that can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf, such as booking, buying or organising, rather than simply answering questions like a chatbot. Because they act as well as respond, they open up new ways for companies to earn money, from subscriptions to commissions on transactions.

Hyperscalers: The handful of giant technology companies that run the world’s largest cloud computing networks and rent out computing power and storage to businesses. They are the biggest buyers of AI chips and data centre equipment, so their spending and results are a key barometer for the whole AI trade.

AI compute: The raw processing power needed to train and run AI models, supplied mainly by specialised chips in large data centres. Rising demand for compute is what drives orders for chipmakers and server builders.

Monetisation: How companies turn AI investment into revenue. Investors have questioned whether the enormous sums spent on data centres will pay off, so evidence of AI-related sales growth is closely watched each earnings season.

Cloud utilisation: How much of a cloud provider’s installed capacity is actually being used and paid for. Higher utilisation means data centre spending is generating revenue rather than sitting idle.

AI server assembler: A manufacturer that builds the complete computer systems housing AI chips, combining processors, memory, cooling and networking into racks for data centres. Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn, is the largest.

Megacap platforms: The very largest listed technology companies, each worth well over a trillion dollars, whose products reach billions of users and give them scale to profit from AI.

Defensive tech: Technology companies with steadier, less cyclical earnings, such as established software or services firms, that tend to hold up better when markets turn volatile.

---

What is hyperscaler cloud growth?

The companies: Hyperscalers are the handful of technology giants that run the world’s largest cloud computing networks, chiefly Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. They rent computing power, storage and AI tools to businesses over the internet, so customers don’t need to build their own data centres.

What the growth figure measures: Hyperscaler cloud growth is the year-on-year increase in revenue from these cloud businesses. Analysts often average it across the main providers to gauge how fast demand for cloud services, and increasingly AI services, is expanding.

Why it matters for AI: The hyperscalers are spending tens of billions of dollars a year on data centres and AI chips. Their cloud revenue growth is the clearest sign of whether that spending is paying off. Faster growth suggests customers are actually using and paying for AI capacity; slowing growth would raise questions about overbuilding.

Why markets watch it: Because the hyperscalers are the biggest buyers of AI chips and servers, their cloud results ripple through the entire AI supply chain, from chipmakers such as TSMC to server builders such as Hon Hai.

Where it stands: UBS expects average hyperscaler cloud revenue growth to accelerate to 58% year on year in the September quarter, up from 48% in the June quarter. The figures will be tested when the major cloud providers report later this month.

"The most advanced AI on the planet and the desk head tells me to go fetch his dry cleaning."

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal
item.description:
For European carmakers, a hybrid quota offers some relief from lower-priced Chinese competition at a time when Volkswagen, Stellantis, Mercedes and BMW are under pressure on profits, though the cap’s generous starting size and annual increases limit how much market share it protects. Chinese brands that have leaned on hybrids to sidestep EU electric vehicle tariffs face slower European growth, with Chery among the most exposed. The bigger risk for markets is Thursday’s summit: a push by Germany and France for broader trade tools could invite retaliation, and Beijing’s control of rare earth supplies gives it leverage over the same European manufacturers the quota is meant to protect.

---

Beijing has given Brussels a hybrid car quota and kept almost everything else, buying time before EU leaders decide how hard to push.

Summary:

  • The EU plans to limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to 350,000 a year, with the quota rising 6% annually from the second year and lasting four years
  • The aim is for the safeguards to apply from December 1; they would technically cover hybrids from all countries to comply with WTO rules, with China’s quota at least as large as any other exporter’s
  • The move follows a 16-point China-EU consensus on trade and investment reached in Beijing on Friday, with further talks planned for January and March
  • Chinese brands took about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August, partly because hybrids escaped the EU’s 2024 tariffs on electric vehicles
  • Analysts see the deal as a win for Beijing, which conceded little on the drivers of an EU trade deficit of more than €1 billion a day
  • EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to consider a tougher response, with Germany and France pushing for stronger trade defence tools

The European Union plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 a year, after Beijing agreed to curb exports as part of a 16-point trade and investment consensus reached in talks that ended on Friday.

The proposed safeguards could take effect from December 1, Bloomberg News reported, citing a document outlining the measures. The quota would rise by 6% a year from the second year and remain in place for four years. To comply with World Trade Organization rules against discrimination, the limits would technically apply to hybrid imports from all countries, with China receiving a quota at least as large as any other exporter. Safeguards of this kind usually take the form of tariff-rate quotas, which leave imports below a set volume untouched and apply a levy to anything above it.

The agreement followed talks in Beijing between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. Chinese hybrid shipments have surged partly because they escaped the tariffs Brussels imposed on fully electric vehicles in 2024, and Chinese brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August. EU ambassadors briefed on Sunday broadly welcomed the outcome but described it as only the start of efforts to rebalance trade.

Analysts were less impressed. One China-focused research firm called the deal a strategic win for Beijing, arguing that beyond vehicles and modest tariff relief it does little to change China’s trading terms with Europe, while buying time for further talks in January and March. A trade law specialist said the timing suggested China wanted to ease tensions before EU leaders meet, and warned that WTO-compliant remedies often have limited impact on overall trade flows.

The stakes for European industry are high. The EU’s trade deficit with China now exceeds €1 billion a day, and European carmakers are among the weakest performers globally. Mercedes-Benz car sales fell 8% in the third quarter, and Volkswagen cut its profit forecast last month. Renault Chief Executive Francois Provost welcomed the deal as a milestone, saying that without it Europe would face a damaging trade war.

EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to decide whether to go further, after Germany and France called for stronger tools, including one that could restrict China’s access to the single market. Beijing has warned against protectionism, and its dominance of rare earth supplies gives it a powerful lever should Europe escalate.

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI preview: energy set to lift inflation to 3.7%, core seen steady at 2.4%
item.description:
Wednesday’s report is a direct read on how far the Iran war’s energy shock is feeding into US consumer prices, and a hot energy component would reinforce the link between crude risk and Fed policy. Treasury markets are likely to trade the core number rather than the headline: a soft core would favour the front end and weigh on the dollar, while a firm one would revive October hike pricing that faded after weak payrolls. Gold would likely benefit from a soft core and lower yields. With Brent still above $100 and fresh attacks on Saudi infrastructure, energy-driven inflation risk extends well beyond this release.

--

September’s CPI is set to look alarming on the surface and calm underneath, and the Fed has to decide which one to believe.

Summary:

  • US September CPI is due Wednesday at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET), the last inflation report before the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting
  • The market expects headline CPI to rise 0.6% on the month, lifting the annual rate to around 3.7% from 3.4%
  • Core inflation is forecast to slow to around 0.2% on the month, holding at 2.4% annually
  • Energy is expected to jump around 5.5%, led by gasoline, while food stays subdued
  • Odds of an October Fed hike have fallen to around one in four after weak September payrolls, with December still largely priced
  • Fed Chair Warsh speaks in Bangkok early Friday, his final scheduled remarks before the meeting

US consumer prices are expected to post their sharpest monthly rise since April when September inflation data is released on Wednesday, driven almost entirely by energy, while underlying inflation is forecast to stay subdued.

The market expects headline CPI to climb 0.6% in September, according to Westpac’s calendar, up from 0.4% in August. That would lift the annual rate to around 3.7% from 3.4%, a four-month high. The Cleveland Fed’s inflation nowcast points in the same direction, at about 0.5% for the month and 3.6% on the year. The report is due at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET).

Energy is the main driver. Analysts expect energy prices to rise around 5.5% in the month, led by gasoline, which would be the largest energy contribution since March. In August, gasoline prices were already up more than 27% on a year earlier.

Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, is expected to tell a calmer story. Forecasts point to a rise of around 0.2%, slower than August’s 0.3%, keeping the annual core rate at 2.4%. August’s core reading was boosted by a one-off jump in telephone services following a methodology change, and analysts expect volatile items such as hotel prices and used cars to correct. Airfares are the exception, rising as higher jet fuel costs pass through to ticket prices.

That split puts the Federal Reserve in an awkward position. The Fed raised its target range to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, but the odds of a follow-up move at the October 27-28 meeting fell to around one in four after September payrolls showed only 29,000 jobs added. Markets still largely price a December hike. Goldman Sachs had expected one more increase in October, though that view assumed oil would fall towards $85, and Brent remains above $100.

A firm core reading alongside the energy-driven headline would likely revive October hike bets, while a soft core would reinforce expectations of a December move. Thursday’s producer prices and retail sales will add to the picture before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok early Friday, his last scheduled appearance before the meeting.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: IEA urges faster diesel releases as 400m-barrel March pledge lags, board meets Oct 15
item.description:
For oil, the IEA’s focus confirms that the acute shortage sits in refined products rather than crude, which points to continued support for diesel margins even as Gulf crude flows recover. The European view that the G7 deal mostly repackages March pledges matters for pricing, since it implies fewer genuinely new barrels than the 100 million headline suggests and limits any relief to tightness. Tenders and the board’s decision this week will set expectations: concrete, front-loaded diesel volumes could cap distillate cracks, while vague commitments risk leaving prices elevated. Fresh disruption to Saudi supply would add pressure to an already strained product market.

--- Seven months after its biggest-ever stock release, the IEA is still chasing barrels, and this time it wants diesel first.

Summary:

  • IEA chief Fatih Birol urged members that have not fully delivered stocks pledged under the March collective action to accelerate releases, prioritising diesel
  • He asked all members, including those that have completed their pledges, to assess whether further diesel releases are needed and to set out scale and timing
  • Birol cited renewed attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, ahead of the agency’s October 15 governing board meeting
  • The G7 agreed this month to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude after the Trump administration threatened Europe with a diesel export ban
  • EU countries broadly see the G7 deal as enacting March commitments rather than adding new volumes
  • In March, the IEA’s 32 members agreed to release 400 million barrels, the largest emergency release on record

The International Energy Agency has urged its members to speed up delivery of emergency oil stocks pledged in March and to consider releasing more diesel, as record fuel prices and fresh attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure tighten global markets.

In a statement ahead of the agency’s October 15 governing board meeting, Executive Director Fatih Birol called on governments that have yet to fully deliver their share of the March collective action to accelerate those releases where possible, with diesel given priority. He also asked all members, including those that have already met their pledges, to assess whether further diesel releases are needed and to set out how large they would be and when they would take place. Birol said current conditions merit immediate attention and are best handled through cooperation among members, pointing to renewed attacks on civilian and energy targets in Saudi Arabia.

The IEA’s 32 members agreed in March to release 400 million barrels from emergency reserves in response to the Iran war, the largest such action in the agency’s history. That some pledged volumes remain undelivered seven months later underlines how drawn out the effort has been.

Pressure has built since. After the Trump administration threatened European countries with a diesel export ban unless they did more to curb record prices, the Group of Seven agreed earlier this month to release as much as 100 million barrels of diesel and crude. European Union members, however, broadly view that deal as putting the March commitments into effect rather than adding new volumes.

The focus on diesel reflects where the strain is greatest. Gulf crude exports have largely recovered, but Goldman Sachs estimates that shipments of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel from the region remain around half of normal. Russia partially lifted its own diesel export ban over the weekend, clearing 500,000 tons for international buyers after an agreement between Presidents Putin and Trump.

The governing board meeting is the next test of whether IEA members can turn pledges into barrels quickly enough to ease record diesel prices, and whether any genuinely new volumes emerge beyond the March commitments.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Preview: RBA minutes and jobs data headline Australia’s week ahead, with unemployment seen at 4.6%
item.description:
For the Australian dollar and front-end rates, the minutes carry more weight than usual because Bullock’s post-meeting tone was softer than the decision itself. A record that leans toward holding would support pricing for a pause and could weigh on the currency, while one that keeps further tightening clearly on the table would reinforce Westpac’s call for another move by year-end. Oil is the swing factor behind both outcomes, as the board explicitly cited Middle East pressure on fuel prices, so any renewed crude strength from Gulf attacks would harden the inflation case. An upside surprise in unemployment would sharpen the market’s focus on downside risks to growth.

---

Four hikes in, the question for Australia this week is whether the RBA’s resolve or its Governor’s softer words better describe where policy goes next.

Summary:

  • Minutes of the RBA’s September meeting, when the cash rate rose 25 basis points to 4.60%, are due Tuesday
  • CBA will be checking whether the minutes match the more dovish tone Governor Bullock struck afterwards, and says the hurdle for another hike is now higher
  • Westpac still expects one more increase, taking the cash rate to 4.85% by December
  • September labour force data on Thursday is expected to show unemployment steady at 4.6%, the highest since late 2021
  • Westpac forecasts 20,000 new jobs, matching consensus, while CBA expects a softer 10,000 after August’s surprise 40,000 gain
  • Consumer sentiment slumped after the September hike, and business conditions turned negative in August

Australia’s week centres on two releases that will shape expectations for the Reserve Bank’s next move: minutes of the September policy meeting on Tuesday and the September labour force survey on Thursday. Both are due at 11:30 am Sydney time, 00:30 GMT (8:30 pm ET the previous evening).

The RBA’s Monetary Policy Board lifted the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% in September, a unanimous and widely expected decision that marked the fourth hike of the cycle. The board said inflation remained too high, pointing to domestic capacity pressures alongside global shocks from the Middle East conflict and the AI investment boom. It acknowledged that the economy was slowing and the labour market loosening, but not quickly enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable timeframe, especially with renewed pressure on oil prices.

CBA says the minutes should shed light on the arguments for holding rates steady, and it will be watching whether they match the more dovish tone Governor Michele Bullock struck at her press conference, when she noted that the four hikes would take time to flow through. CBA views the hurdle for another increase as now higher. Westpac takes a firmer line, forecasting one more hike to 4.85% by December, and says markets will look to the minutes for guidance on the outlook.

The hike has already hit households. Westpac’s consumer sentiment index fell 4.7% to 80.4 in October, near the weakest levels in the survey’s history, with confidence among those surveyed after the decision far below those polled before it.

Thursday’s jobs data follows a surprise jump of around 40,000 in August that nevertheless pushed unemployment up to 4.6%, the highest since late 2021, as participation rose to 67.1%, just below its record. Westpac forecasts a 20,000 rise in September, in line with consensus, with participation easing to 67.0% and unemployment steady at 4.6%. It says cost-of-living pressures and higher rates are drawing more people into the workforce, keeping labour supply ahead of demand.

CBA expects a smaller 10,000 gain, noting its own internal data had jobs growth closer to 20,000 a month, and also sees unemployment at 4.6%. It warns the print could be noisier than usual: a survey group with a very low jobless rate is rotating out, an upside risk, while August’s rise may have been overstated and could partly reverse. CBA cautions against reading any fall in unemployment as a change in trend, expecting the rate to drift higher as the economy slows.

Elsewhere, the NAB business survey on Tuesday follows August’s slide in conditions into negative territory for the first time in six years.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman: Gulf oil exports back at 22-23 mb/d, but Dated Brent stays very high
item.description:
For oil, the split between recovering volumes and stubbornly high physical prices is the key tension. Restored crude flows argue for lower benchmark prices over time, but the premium in Dated Brent shows buyers are still paying up for prompt barrels to rebuild depleted inventories, which keeps the front of the curve steeply backwardated. Refined products remain the tightest corner, supporting diesel and jet margins even as crude supply normalises. The weekend’s Houthi claims against Saudi Aramco facilities are an immediate test, since Saudi barrels have led the recovery, and any confirmed disruption would likely widen the physical premium again.

---

The barrels are back, but the fear isn’t: Gulf exports have normalised while physical buyers keep paying war prices.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs estimates Persian Gulf oil exports, including dark exports, recovered to 22-23 mb/d over the past two weeks, broadly in line with their 2025 average
  • Physical Dated Brent prices remain very high despite the recovery
  • Crude has driven the rebound, with Saudi Arabia leading and Iran showing no seaborne crude exports in September
  • JPMorgan’s estimate is more conservative, at around 89% of 2025 levels, mainly due to how dark flows are counted
  • Exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel remain at roughly half of normal levels
  • Goldman still expects Brent to ease to $85 by year-end and $80 in 2027

Oil exports from the Persian Gulf have returned to roughly normal levels, but physical crude prices have yet to follow, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank estimates that Gulf exports, including so-called dark exports, have recovered to 22 to 23 million barrels per day over the past two weeks, broadly in line with their 2025 average, while physical Dated Brent remains very high.

Dark exports are cargoes carried by tankers that switch off their satellite transponders, making them hard to track. Goldman estimated these flows at around 5 million barrels per day in September, a large part of why its count is higher than others. JPMorgan, using a more conservative approach, put recent Gulf exports at about 89% of 2025 levels, with most of the difference coming down to how much of the dark fleet is included.

The recovery has been led by crude rather than refined products. In late September, Goldman said crude exports had climbed above their 2025 average, with Saudi shipments more than doubling during the month to nearly 12 million barrels per day and the UAE also exporting above normal. Satellite data showed no seaborne crude exports from Iran. Products are lagging badly: exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel remain around half of normal, which Goldman attributes to elevated regional refinery outages and the greater risk faced by smaller product tankers carrying more flammable cargo.

Physical prices tell a different story to the flow data. Dated Brent, the price for North Sea cargoes loading on specific dates, was recently near $120 a barrel, well above futures. Goldman links the gap to fears that escalation could damage long-term production and to record-low global stocks outside OECD commercial inventories, which have prompted buyers to rebuild supplies quickly. The bank estimates the risk premium in Brent spreads averaged $22 a barrel in September, the second-highest monthly level on record and above the peak during the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war.

Goldman maintains its base case that Brent eases to $85 by year-end and $80 in 2027, while warning that renewed escalation could push prices sharply higher. The weekend’s Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities put that risk directly against the barrels that have driven the recovery.

Dated Brent is the spot price for physical North Sea cargoes loading on specific dates, as opposed to the front-month futures contract; in early April the spot premium over futures exceeded $25 a barrel. Normally that spread is narrow.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
